claim: Male moths possess highly sensitive and selective olfactory systems that detect sex pheromones produced by their females.
source: Male moths possess highly sensitive and selective olfactory systems that detect sex pheromones produced by their females.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to prior work (Schneider, 1964; Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011).

claim: Pheromone receptors (PRs) play a key role in detecting sex pheromones.
source: Pheromone receptors (PRs) play a key role in this process.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Leal, 2013; Sakurai et al., 2004).

claim: HassOr14b is tuned to (Z)−9-hexadecenal, the major sex-pheromone component in Helicoverpa assulta.
source: The PR HassOr14b is found to be tuned to (Z)−9-hexadecenal, the major sex-pheromone component, in Helicoverpa assulta.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from Xenopus oocyte expression and electrophysiology (Figure 3A, Figure 4).

claim: HassOr14b is co-localized with HassOr6 or HassOr16 in two olfactory sensory neurons within the same sensilla.
source: HassOr14b is co-localized with HassOr6 or HassOr16 in two olfactory sensory neurons within the same sensilla.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: HarmOr14b, the ortholog of HassOr14b in Helicoverpa armigera, is tuned to (Z)−9-tetradecenal.
source: As HarmOr14b, the ortholog of HassOr14b in the closely related species Helicoverpa armigera, is tuned to another chemical (Z)−9-tetradecenal, we study the amino acid residues that determine their ligand selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by functional data from Xenopus oocyte expression (Figure 3B) and prior studies (Jiang et al., 2014).

claim: Two amino acids F232I and T355I together determine the functional difference between HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.
source: Two amino acids located in the intracellular domains F232I and T355I together determine the functional difference between the two orthologs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional analysis (Figure 8C, F, I).

claim: Species-specific changes in the tuning specificity of PRs in the two Helicoverpa moth species could be achieved with just a few amino acid substitutions.
source: We conclude that species-specific changes in the tuning specificity of the PRs in the two Helicoverpa moth species could be achieved with just a few amino acid substitutions, which provides new insights into the evolution of closely related moth species.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that two amino acid changes can shift receptor specificity.

claim: Most moth sex pheromones have multiple components present in specific ratios that play significant roles in intraspecific sexual communication and in interspecific reproductive isolation.
source: Most moth sex pheromones have multiple components present in specific ratios that play significant roles in intraspecific sexual communication and in interspecific reproductive isolation (Cardé et al., 1977).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Male moths possess highly sensitive and selective olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) located in antennal sensilla that detect the pheromone molecules.
source: Male moths possess highly sensitive and selective olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) located in antennal sensilla that detect the pheromone molecules (Schneider, 1964; Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pheromone receptors (PRs) located in the dendritic membrane of OSNs play a pivotal role in peripheral coding of sex pheromones.
source: Pheromone receptors (PRs) located in the dendritic membrane of OSNs play a pivotal role in peripheral coding of sex pheromones (Leal, 2013; Sakurai et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PRs are in general narrowly tuned to specific pheromone components.
source: Unlike general odorant receptors (ORs) that typically bind more than one ligand (de Fouchier et al., 2017), PRs are in general narrowly tuned to specific pheromone components (Grosse-Wilde et al., 2007; Miura et al., 2010; Zhang and Löfstedt, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Closely related moth species often use combinations of the same or similar pheromone components, which is a reflection of their common evolutionary history.
source: Closely related moth species often use combinations of the same or similar pheromone components, which is a reflection of their common evolutionary history (Cardé and Haynes, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A single-point mutation in a PR is responsible for its different specificities in Ostrinia furnacalis and Ostrinia nubilalis.
source: The single study to date that has addressed this question showed that a single-point mutation in a PR is responsible for its different specificities in Ostrinia furnacalis and Ostrinia nubilalis (Leary et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citation.

claim: The determinant amino acids for OR specificity are located mainly in transmembrane domains and extracellular loops.
source: Studies of a number of ORs in D. melanogaster and Anopheles gambiae indicated that the determinant amino acids are located mainly in transmembrane domains and extracellular loops (Guo and Kim, 2010; Hughes et al., 2014; Nichols and Luetje, 2010; Pellegrino et al., 2011), but the molecular mechanisms that determine the ligand selectivity of ORs are still unclear.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Helicoverpa assulta is a specialist mainly feeding on solanaceous plants, including tobacco and hot pepper.
source: The former is a specialist mainly feeding on solanaceous plants, including tobacco and hot pepper, whereas the latter is a polyphagous species and is one of the most devastating pests in the world.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the species.

claim: Helicoverpa armigera is a polyphagous species and is one of the most devastating pests in the world.
source: The former is a specialist mainly feeding on solanaceous plants, including tobacco and hot pepper, whereas the latter is a polyphagous species and is one of the most devastating pests in the world.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the species.

claim: H. assulta and H. armigera share two compounds, (Z)−9-hexadecenal (Z9-16:Ald) and (Z)−11-hexadecenal (Z11-16:Ald) as their principal sex-pheromone components, but in inverse ratios, 93:7 and 3:97, respectively.
source: H. assulta and H. armigera share two compounds, (Z)−9-hexadecenal (Z9-16:Ald) and (Z)−11-hexadecenal (Z11-16:Ald) as their principal sex-pheromone components, but in inverse ratios, 93:7 and 3:97, respectively (Piccardi et al., 1977; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: (Z)−9-tetradecenal (Z9-14:Ald) acts as an antagonist in the pheromone communication of H. assulta.
source: (Z)−9-tetradecenal (Z9-14:Ald) acts as an antagonist in the pheromone communication of H. assulta (Boo et al., 1995; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In H. armigera, Z9-14:Ald acts as an agonist in small amounts (0.3%).
source: In that of H. armigera, Z9-14:Ald acts as an agonist in small amounts (0.3%) (Rothschild, 1978; Wu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012) but an antagonist in higher amounts (1% and above) (Gothilf et al., 1978; Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In H. armigera, Z9-14:Ald acts as an antagonist in higher amounts (1% and above).
source: In that of H. armigera, Z9-14:Ald acts as an agonist in small amounts (0.3%) (Rothschild, 1978; Wu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012) but an antagonist in higher amounts (1% and above) (Gothilf et al., 1978; Kehat and Dunkelblum, 1990; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Three functional types of pheromone-sensitive sensilla, A, B and C, can be distinguished in the male antennae of H. assulta and H. armigera.
source: Three functional types of pheromone-sensitive sensilla, A, B and C, can be distinguished in the male antennae of the two species (Baker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Sensilla type A specifically respond to Z11-16:Ald.
source: Sensilla type A specifically respond to Z11-16:Ald, type B respond to Z9-14:Ald, and type C respond to Z9-16:Ald, Z9-14:Ald and some other structurally related compounds.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation (Baker et al., 2004).

claim: Sensilla type B respond to Z9-14:Ald.
source: Sensilla type A specifically respond to Z11-16:Ald, type B respond to Z9-14:Ald, and type C respond to Z9-16:Ald, Z9-14:Ald and some other structurally related compounds.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation (Baker et al., 2004).

claim: Sensilla type C respond to Z9-16:Ald, Z9-14:Ald and some other structurally related compounds.
source: Sensilla type A specifically respond to Z11-16:Ald, type B respond to Z9-14:Ald, and type C respond to Z9-16:Ald, Z9-14:Ald and some other structurally related compounds.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation (Baker et al., 2004).

claim: The population of A-type sensilla predominates in males of H. armigera.
source: The population of A-type sensilla predominates in males of H. armigera, while C-type sensilla are most numerous in males of H. assulta (Wu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: C-type sensilla are most numerous in males of H. assulta.
source: The population of A-type sensilla predominates in males of H. armigera, while C-type sensilla are most numerous in males of H. assulta (Wu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HarmOr13 and HassOr13 are specifically tuned to Z11-16:Ald.
source: Previous functional studies of the PRs showed that HarmOr13 and HassOr13 are specifically tuned to Z11-16:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr14b and HassOr16 are tuned to Z9-14:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr16 is tuned to both Z9-14:Ald and (Z)−11-hexadecenol (Z11-16:OH) (Liu et al., 2013), while HarmOr6 and HassOr6 are mainly tuned to (Z)−9-hexadecenol (Z9-16:OH) (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citations.

claim: HarmOr14b and HassOr16 are tuned to Z9-14:Ald.
source: Previous functional studies of the PRs showed that HarmOr13 and HassOr13 are specifically tuned to Z11-16:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr14b and HassOr16 are tuned to Z9-14:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr16 is tuned to both Z9-14:Ald and (Z)−11-hexadecenol (Z11-16:OH) (Liu et al., 2013), while HarmOr6 and HassOr6 are mainly tuned to (Z)−9-hexadecenol (Z9-16:OH) (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citations.

claim: HarmOr16 is tuned to both Z9-14:Ald and (Z)−11-hexadecenol (Z11-16:OH).
source: Previous functional studies of the PRs showed that HarmOr13 and HassOr13 are specifically tuned to Z11-16:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr14b and HassOr16 are tuned to Z9-14:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr16 is tuned to both Z9-14:Ald and (Z)−11-hexadecenol (Z11-16:OH) (Liu et al., 2013), while HarmOr6 and HassOr6 are mainly tuned to (Z)−9-hexadecenol (Z9-16:OH) (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citations.

claim: HarmOr6 and HassOr6 are mainly tuned to (Z)−9-hexadecenol (Z9-16:OH).
source: Previous functional studies of the PRs showed that HarmOr13 and HassOr13 are specifically tuned to Z11-16:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr14b and HassOr16 are tuned to Z9-14:Ald (Jiang et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013), HarmOr16 is tuned to both Z9-14:Ald and (Z)−11-hexadecenol (Z11-16:OH) (Liu et al., 2013), while HarmOr6 and HassOr6 are mainly tuned to (Z)−9-hexadecenol (Z9-16:OH) (Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citations.

claim: The phylogenetic tree of PRs was clustered into seven lineages: Or16, Or6, Or14b, Or14, Or15, Or11, and Or13.
source: In general, the tree was clustered into seven lineages, Or16, Or6, Or14b, Or14, Or15, Or11, and Or13.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Or14b cluster specifically occurs in H. assulta and H. armigera.
source: Each lineage contains the PR(s) from Helicoverpa and other noctuids except for Or14b, suggesting that the Or14b cluster specifically occurs in H. assulta and H. armigera.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 1.

claim: All PRs and Orcos analyzed in this study are subjected to purifying selection.
source: The ω values < 1 were observed in all PR clusters and the Orco cluster (cluster Or16: ω <0.21; cluster Or6: ω <0.19; cluster Or14b: ω = 0.17; cluster Or14: ω <0.15; cluster Or15: ω = 0.13; cluster Or11: ω <0.13; cluster Or13, ω <0.17; cluster Orco: ω <0.03); this indicates that all the PRs and Orcos analyzed in this study are subjected to purifying selection, which is consistent with the previous studies (Zhang and Löfstedt, 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by dN/dS ratio analysis shown in Figure 1 and cited prior work.

claim: All candidate PRs were male-specific except for Or11, which was highly expressed in both male and female antennae.
source: All the candidate PRs were male-specific except for Or11, which was highly expressed in both male and female antennae (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the male antennae of H. assulta, HassOr14b had the highest expression level, nearly twofold higher than the levels of HassOr6 and HassOr16, and five- to sixfold greater than that of HassOr13.
source: In the male antennae of H. assulta, HassOr14b had the highest expression level, nearly twofold higher than the levels of HassOr6 and HassOr16, and five- to sixfold greater than that of HassOr13 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: HassOr14b is specifically expressed in the male antennae and its expression level is the highest among the PRs.
source: The values of fragments per kilobase of transcript per million reads (FPKM) in different tissues of H. assulta further demonstrated that HassOr14b is specifically expressed in the male antennae and that its expression level is the highest among the PRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FPKM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the male antennae of H. armigera, HarmOr13 and HarmOr11 showed the highest expression level, which was about five- to sixfold higher than HarmOr16 and HarmOr14.
source: In the male antennae of H. armigera, HarmOr13 and HarmOr11 showed the highest expression level, which was about five- to sixfold higher than HarmOr16 and HarmOr14; HarmOr14b had a low expression level, even lower than HarmOr16 and HarmOr6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: HarmOr14b had a low expression level in H. armigera, even lower than HarmOr16 and HarmOr6.
source: In the male antennae of H. armigera, HarmOr13 and HarmOr11 showed the highest expression level, which was about five- to sixfold higher than HarmOr16 and HarmOr14; HarmOr14b had a low expression level, even lower than HarmOr16 and HarmOr6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Oocytes expressing HassOr14b/HassOrco responded robustly to Z9-16:Ald, and to a much lesser extent to Z9-16:OH at a concentration of 10–4 M.
source: Oocytes expressing HassOr14b/HassOrco responded robustly to Z9-16:Ald, and to a much lesser extent to Z9-16:OH at a concentration of 10–4 M (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Z9-16:Ald induced currents increasing from the lowest threshold concentration of 10−6 M to 3.3 × 10–3 M in a dose-dependent manner with an EC50 value of 8.65 × 10–5 M for HassOr14b.
source: Z9-16:Ald induced currents increasing from the lowest threshold concentration of 10−6 M to 3.3 × 10–3 M in a dose-dependent manner with an EC50 value of 8.65 × 10–5 M (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4.

claim: HarmOr14b is specifically tuned to Z9-14:Ald, and also weakly responds to Z9-16:Ald.
source: As previously reported (Jiang et al., 2014), we verified that HarmOr14b is specifically tuned to Z9-14:Ald, and also weakly responds to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 3B), while HassOr6 is mainly tuned to Z9-16:OH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and HassOr16 is specific for Z9-14:Ald (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B and cited prior work.

claim: HassOr6 is mainly tuned to Z9-16:OH.
source: As previously reported (Jiang et al., 2014), we verified that HarmOr14b is specifically tuned to Z9-14:Ald, and also weakly responds to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 3B), while HassOr6 is mainly tuned to Z9-16:OH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and HassOr16 is specific for Z9-14:Ald (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HassOr16 is specific for Z9-14:Ald.
source: As previously reported (Jiang et al., 2014), we verified that HarmOr14b is specifically tuned to Z9-14:Ald, and also weakly responds to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 3B), while HassOr6 is mainly tuned to Z9-16:OH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and HassOr16 is specific for Z9-14:Ald (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HassOr14b and HassOr6 were co-localized in some sensilla.
source: We found that HassOr14b and HassOr6 were co-localized in some sensilla (arrows, Figure 5A1–4), while in other sensilla only HassOr14b was detected (arrows, Figure 5B1–4).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A1-4.

claim: In some sensilla only HassOr14b was detected.
source: We found that HassOr14b and HassOr6 were co-localized in some sensilla (arrows, Figure 5A1–4), while in other sensilla only HassOr14b was detected (arrows, Figure 5B1–4).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B1-4.

claim: HassOr14b and HassOr16 were co-localized in some sensilla.
source: A similar situation was observed for HassOr14b and HassOr16. They were co-localized in some sensilla (arrows, Figure 5C1–4), but only HassOr14b was detected in other sensilla (arrows, Figure 5D1–4).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C1-4.

claim: In some sensilla only HassOr14b was detected (not HassOr16).
source: A similar situation was observed for HassOr14b and HassOr16. They were co-localized in some sensilla (arrows, Figure 5C1–4), but only HassOr14b was detected in other sensilla (arrows, Figure 5D1–4).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5D1-4.

claim: HassOr6 and HassOr16 were always expressed in different sensilla.
source: However, HassOr6 and HassOr16 were always expressed in different sensilla (arrows, Figure 5E1–4).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5E1-4.

claim: HassOr14b and HarmOr14b exhibit 91% amino acid identity (402 out of 440).
source: HassOr14b and HarmOr14b exhibit 91% amino acid identity (402 out of 440, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but their ligand selectivity is different.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 38 differing amino acids between HassOr14b and HarmOr14b were distributed fairly uniformly in the two proteins.
source: From the sequence alignment and secondary structural analysis (Figure 6; TOPCONS, topcons.net), we found that the 38 differing amino acids were distributed fairly uniformly in the two proteins.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ligand selectivity of HassOr14b was changed remarkably by replacement of the region VI.
source: Interestingly, comparing with the ligand selectivity of the wild type (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), we observed that the ligand selectivity of HassOr14b was changed remarkably by replacement of the region VI or VIII. HassOr14b after replacing the region VI had a significantly higher response to Z9-14:Ald than to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 7F), while after replacing the region VIII had strong responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: HassOr14b after replacing the region VI had a significantly higher response to Z9-14:Ald than to Z9-16:Ald.
source: Interestingly, comparing with the ligand selectivity of the wild type (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), we observed that the ligand selectivity of HassOr14b was changed remarkably by replacement of the region VI or VIII. HassOr14b after replacing the region VI had a significantly higher response to Z9-14:Ald than to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 7F), while after replacing the region VIII had strong responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: HassOr14b after replacing the region VIII had strong responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald.
source: Interestingly, comparing with the ligand selectivity of the wild type (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), we observed that the ligand selectivity of HassOr14b was changed remarkably by replacement of the region VI or VIII. HassOr14b after replacing the region VI had a significantly higher response to Z9-14:Ald than to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 7F), while after replacing the region VIII had strong responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Replacement of the regions I or III produced significantly lower responses to Z9-16:Ald.
source: In particular, replacement of the regions I or III produced significantly lower responses to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 7A and C), while replacement of the region VII resulted in a significantly stronger response to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: Replacement of the region VII resulted in a significantly stronger response to Z9-16:Ald.
source: In particular, replacement of the regions I or III produced significantly lower responses to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 7A and C), while replacement of the region VII resulted in a significantly stronger response to Z9-16:Ald (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Replacement of the regions II, IV or V did not affect the selectivity of the receptor with reference to the wild-type.
source: Replacement of the regions II, IV or V did not affect the selectivity of the receptor with reference to the wild-type (Figure 7B,D and E).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 7B, D, and E.

claim: Five amino acids (E188G, E196D, F232I, R262K, and R270K) in the region VI differ between HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.
source: Five amino acids (E188G, E196D, F232I, R262K, and R270K) in the region VI, and three (T355I, R395K, and A425K) in the region VIII were different between HassOr14b and HarmOr14b (Figures 6 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Three amino acids (T355I, R395K, and A425K) in the region VIII differ between HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.
source: Five amino acids (E188G, E196D, F232I, R262K, and R270K) in the region VI, and three (T355I, R395K, and A425K) in the region VIII were different between HassOr14b and HarmOr14b (Figures 6 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: The mutant F232I was activated more by Z9-14:Ald than by Z9-16:Ald.
source: Comparing with the wild type (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), we found that the mutant F232I was activated more by Z9-14:Ald than by Z9-16:Ald (Figure 8C), while the mutant T355I showed very strong responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The mutant T355I showed very strong responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald.
source: Comparing with the wild type (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), we found that the mutant F232I was activated more by Z9-14:Ald than by Z9-16:Ald (Figure 8C), while the mutant T355I showed very strong responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: E196D and R262K still responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed a decrease in current compared to the wild type.
source: Compared to the wild type, E196D and R262K still responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed a decrease in current (Figure 8B and D), E188G and R270K also responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed an increase in current (Figure 8A and E), while R395K and A425K exhibited the same response level to Z9-16:Ald and, to a minor extent, to Z9-14:Ald (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 8B and D.

claim: E188G and R270K responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed an increase in current compared to the wild type.
source: Compared to the wild type, E196D and R262K still responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed a decrease in current (Figure 8B and D), E188G and R270K also responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed an increase in current (Figure 8A and E), while R395K and A425K exhibited the same response level to Z9-16:Ald and, to a minor extent, to Z9-14:Ald (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 8A and E.

claim: R395K and A425K exhibited the same response level to Z9-16:Ald and, to a minor extent, to Z9-14:Ald.
source: Compared to the wild type, E196D and R262K still responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed a decrease in current (Figure 8B and D), E188G and R270K also responded to Z9-16:Ald but showed an increase in current (Figure 8A and E), while R395K and A425K exhibited the same response level to Z9-16:Ald and, to a minor extent, to Z9-14:Ald (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 8G and H.

claim: The two-site mutant (F232I + T355I) showed a robust response to Z9-14:Ald and a minor response to Z9-16:Ald, reproducing the characteristic selectivity of HarmOr14b.
source: This two-site mutant showed a robust response to Z9-14:Ald and a minor response to Z9-16:Ald, reproducing the characteristic selectivity of HarmOr14b (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Two single-point mutations, F232I and T355I, located in the intracellular domains of the receptor, together determine the functional shift between HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.
source: In this study, we identify HassOr14b as the PR tuned to Z9-16:Ald, the major sex-pheromone component of H. assulta. Its ortholog HarmOr14b is specific for Z9-14:Ald in H. armigera and we further demonstrate that two single-point mutations, F232I and T355I, located in the intracellular domains of the receptor, together determine the functional shift between orthologs in the two closely related species.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by mutagenesis and functional data (Figure 8C, F, I).

claim: C type sensilla responding to Z9-16:Ald are predominant in male antennae of H. assulta.
source: The previous studies clarified that the C type sensilla responding to Z9-16:Ald are predominant in male antennae of H. assulta (Wu et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2016), the PR tuning to Z9-16:Ald must be highly expressed in male antennae.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The two closely related species not only changed Or14b's expressing level, but also altered its tuning selectivity.
source: This suggests that the two closely related species not only changed Or14b's expressing level, but also altered its tuning selectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression and functional data comparing HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.

claim: There are different combinations of the PRs in the C type sensilla.
source: Our results indicate that there are different combinations of the PRs in the C type sensilla, which is consistent with the previous single sensillum recording results that there are subtypes in the type C sensilla (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from in situ hybridization data (Figure 5) and supported by prior work.

claim: Various combinations of PRs are the molecular basis for the different sensilla subtypes in moth species.
source: Our results indicate that there are different combinations of the PRs in the C type sensilla, which is consistent with the previous single sensillum recording results that there are subtypes in the type C sensilla (Xu et al., 2016). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that shows the various combinations of PRs were the molecular basis for the different sensilla subtypes in moth species.
evidence: This is inferred from in situ hybridization data (Figure 5).

claim: Insect ORs require the co-expression of a ligand-selective OR and a universal odorant co-receptor (Orco) to form ligand-gated ion channels.
source: Insect ORs require the co-expression of a ligand-selective OR and a universal odorant co-receptor (Orco) to form ligand-gated ion channels (Missbach et al., 2014; Vosshall and Hansson, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A single amino acid mutation located in the predicted third TMD could change the ligand specificity of a PR between that of the Asian corn borer and that of the European corn borer.
source: Leary et al. reported that a single amino acid mutation located in the predicted third TMD could change the ligand specificity of a PR between that of the Asian corn borer and that of the European corn borer (Leary et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citation.

claim: A single natural polymorphism of D. melanogaster Or59B in the third transmembrane domain altered DEET sensitivity.
source: Pellegrino et al. showed that a single natural polymorphism of D. melanogaster Or59B in the third transmembrane domain altered DEET sensitivity (Pellegrino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citation.

claim: A single mutation of AgOr15 at the interface between ECL2 and TMD4 produced large changes in responses to odors.
source: In A. gambiae, a single mutation of AgOr15 at the interface between ECL2 and TMD4, produced large changes in responses to odors (Hughes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by citation.

claim: Two single-point mutations, T355I and F232I, are responsible for the different ligand selectivities of HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.
source: By further replacing single amino acids in the two regions, we finally detected two single-point mutations, T355I and F232I responsible for the different ligand selectivities of HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by site-directed mutagenesis and functional data (Figure 8C, F, I).

claim: It is for the first time to find that the two mutation sites in the intracellular domains (ICDs) rather than in the TMDs and ECLs were involved in determination of ligand selectivity.
source: It is for the first time to find that the two mutation sites in the intracellular domains (ICDs) rather than in the TMDs and ECLs were involved in determination of ligand selectivity.
evidence: This is a novel finding inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that F232I and T355I are in ICDs.

claim: The binding site of ligand-specific ORs, such as PRs, may have a complex structure, which involves TMDs, ECLs and ICDs.
source: We suggest two possible explanations for the role of ICDs. First, the binding site of ligand-specific ORs, such as PRs, may have a complex structure, which involves TMDs (Leary et al., 2012), ECLs (Hughes et al., 2014) and ICDs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the role of ICDs in ligand selectivity.

claim: ICDs may be involved in the specific interactions of the PR with the related G proteins.
source: Alternatively, ICDs may be involved in the specific interactions of the PR with the related G proteins. To relay the signal into the cell interior, binding of an extracellular molecule to an OR is tightly followed by binding of the receptor to a trimeric G protein inside the cell (Ignatious Raja et al., 2014; Wicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the role of ICDs, supported by citations about G protein interactions.

claim: Under stabilizing selection, variation of the female pheromone blend is limited, and the males typically prefer the most common pheromone blends.
source: Under stabilizing selection, variation of the female pheromone blend is limited, and the males typically prefer the most common pheromone blends (Groot et al., 2016; Roelofs et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PRs would be subjected to purifying selection.
source: The ω value for all clusters of PRs analyzed in this study are less than 1, suggesting that PRs would be subjected to purifying selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the dN/dS ratio analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: H. assulta is ancestral to H. armigera.
source: Based on previous studies, suggesting that H. assulta is ancestral to H. armigera (Cho et al., 2008; Fang et al., 1997), we tried to reproduce the assumed evolutionary process that mutated HassOr14b into HarmOr14b.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Most of the regional replacements and site mutations did not change the ligand selectivity of HassOr14b, indicating the functional stability of this PR.
source: Most of the regional replacements and site mutations did not change the ligand selectivity of HassOr14b, indicating the functional stability of this PR.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Only F232I and T355I substitutions produced a large change of the ligand selectivity of Or14b, from Z9-16:Ald in H. assulta to Z9-14:Ald in H. armigera.
source: Only F232I and T355I substitutions produced a large change of the ligand selectivity of Or14b, from Z9-16:Ald in H. assulta to Z9-14:Ald in H. armigera.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data (Figure 8C, F, I).

claim: The F232I site mutation produced a small shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald in the response spectrum.
source: The former site mutation produced a small shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald in the response spectrum, the latter extended and strengthened the responses to both chemicals, while the two mutations together generated a complete functional shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data (Figure 8C).

claim: The T355I mutation extended and strengthened the responses to both Z9-16:Ald and Z9-14:Ald.
source: The former site mutation produced a small shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald in the response spectrum, the latter extended and strengthened the responses to both chemicals, while the two mutations together generated a complete functional shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data (Figure 8F).

claim: The two mutations F232I and T355I together generated a complete functional shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald.
source: The former site mutation produced a small shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald in the response spectrum, the latter extended and strengthened the responses to both chemicals, while the two mutations together generated a complete functional shift from Z9-16:Ald to Z9-14:Ald.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and functional data (Figure 8I).

claim: The substitutions of a few key amino acids are able to greatly change PR selectivity, laying the molecular foundations for PR plasticity.
source: These results indicate that the substitutions of a few key amino acids are able to greatly change PR selectivity, laying the molecular foundations for PR plasticity.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that two amino acid changes can shift receptor specificity.

claim: At least two steps, involving in the functional extension and shift, are required for a major functional change of HassOr14b, each step with a single point mutation.
source: Moreover, it seems that at least two steps, involving in the functional extension and shift, are required for a major functional change of HassOr14b, each step with a single point mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that F232I and T355I have different effects individually and together.

claim: In the course of speciation, the functional change of ORs could be a process with multiple amino acid mutations, a few making drastic changes and many making small modifications or even no change in function.
source: In the course of speciation, the functional change of ORs could be a process with multiple amino acid mutations, a few making drastic changes and many making small modifications or even no change in function.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Peripheral coding of the binary blends with reversed ratios is mainly attributed to two group of specific OSNs in separate antennal sensilla with reverse population sizes, which reflect different expression levels of related PRs.
source: Peripheral coding of the binary blends with reversed ratios is mainly attributed to two group of specific OSNs in separate antennal sensilla with reverse population sizes, which reflect different expression levels of related PRs (Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The peripheral modifications of the two closely related species took place in both PR expression level and PR tuning selectivity.
source: The peripheral modifications of the two closely related species took place in both PR expression level and PR tuning selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the expression and functional data comparing HassOr14b and HarmOr14b.

claim: HassOr14b is the most highly expressed PR in male antennae of H. assulta.
source: We found that HassOr14b is the most highly expressed in H. assulta, while HarmOr14b has relatively low expression level in H. armigera.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: HarmOr14b has relatively low expression level in H. armigera.
source: We found that HassOr14b is the most highly expressed in H. assulta, while HarmOr14b has relatively low expression level in H. armigera.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Water-injected oocytes fail to respond to any of the pheromone component stimuli as negative controls.
source: Water-injected oocytes fail to respond to any of the pheromone component stimuli as negative controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
